content: This is an updated version of a Cochrane review originally published in 2015. Severe myoclonic epilepsy in infants (SMEI), also known as Dravet syndrome, is a rare and treatment-resistant form of epilepsy. Stiripentol (STP) has recently been approved as an add-on therapy for this condition. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and tolerability of STP and other antiepileptic treatments, including the ketogenic diet, in patients with SMEI. For the latest update, searches were conducted in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Epilepsy Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and ClinicalTrials.gov, up to December 20, 2016. The World Health Organization's International Clinical Trials Registry Platform was also previously searched, but it was not usable for this update. Additional references were identified through bibliographies, handsearching journals, and conference proceedings. No language restrictions were applied. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-randomized controlled trials, whether double-blinded, single-blinded, or unblinded, as well as parallel-group studies. Eligible studies involved the administration of at least one antiepileptic drug, either as monotherapy or add-on therapy, compared to placebo or no add-on treatment. The outcomes assessed included a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency, seizure freedom, adverse effects, dropout rates, and quality of life. Data were analyzed using Mantel-Haenszel meta-analysis to calculate risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). No new studies were identified since the last version of the review. Specifically, no RCTs were found that evaluated drugs other than STP. The review included two RCTs that assessed the use of STP, involving a total of 64 children. Both studies were judged to have an unclear risk of bias. A significantly higher proportion of participants in the STP group achieved a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency compared to the placebo group (22 out of 33 participants in the STP group versus 2 out of 31 in the placebo group; RR 10.40, 95% CI 2.64 to 40.87). Similarly, a significantly higher proportion of participants in the STP group achieved seizure freedom compared to the placebo group (12 out of 33 participants in the STP group versus 1 out of 31 in the placebo group; RR 7.93, 95% CI 1.52 to 41.21). There were no significant differences in dropout rates between the STP group and the placebo group (2 out of 33 participants in the STP group versus 8 out of 31 in the placebo group; RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.06 to 1.03). However, one study explicitly reported side effects, noting that all participants in the STP group experienced side effects compared to 25% of participants in the placebo group (RR 3.73, 95% CI 1.81 to 7.67). The quality of the evidence was rated as low to moderate according to GRADE criteria, primarily because most of the information came from studies with an unclear risk of bias. In conclusion, data from two small RCTs suggest that STP is significantly more effective than placebo in achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency and seizure freedom in patients with SMEI. However, adverse effects were more common in the STP group. Further well-powered studies with long-term follow-up are needed to definitively establish the long-term efficacy and tolerability of STP in treating SMEI.
